mcqs.question: In `Board.reveal(cell)`, why does the flood-fill recursion only continue through cells with an adjacent-mine count of exactly zero?
options: Because cells with a nonzero count are always mines themselves
Because Java's recursion depth limit is set to exactly the number of zero-count cells

Because a nonzero count means the player needs that number as information to reason about nearby mines — revealing further would give away more than one click's worth of information without any indication of danger
Because it prevents the player from ever flagging a cell
mcqs.explanation: A cell with a nonzero adjacent-mine count is a boundary — it gives the player real information about nearby danger, so the fill should stop and let the player decide the next move rather than auto-revealing past it. A nonzero count doesn't mean the cell itself is a mine (mines are never auto-revealed as part of a fill), there's no such Java-specific recursion limit, and flagging is unrelated to this rule.

mcqs.question: When should you prefer an iterative BFS/queue-based reveal over a simple recursive flood-fill?
options: Always — recursion is never appropriate for tree or graph traversal
Only when the board has more mines than safe cells
Only when supporting a hexagonal grid instead of a square one
When the board can be very large, since a huge connected zero-region could exhaust the call stack with one recursive frame per cell
mcqs.explanation: The real risk with recursive flood-fill is stack depth on a very large connected region — an iterative queue avoids that risk entirely regardless of board size. Recursion is a fine, often more readable choice at typical sizes; mine-to-safe-cell ratio and grid shape (hex vs square) don't determine which reveal strategy to use.

mcqs.question: Why should win detection use a `remainingSafeCells` counter instead of scanning the whole board after each reveal?
options: Because a counter turns win detection into an O(1) check, while a full-board scan after every reveal (including flood-fills that reveal many cells at once) repeats unnecessary work as the board grows
Because scanning the whole board would incorrectly count flagged cells as revealed
Because the counter is required to compute each cell's adjacent-mine count
Because Board cannot be scanned more than once without resetting it
mcqs.explanation: A running counter decremented on each successful safe reveal makes the win check constant-time, avoiding repeated full-board scans that get more expensive as the board grows and as flood-fills reveal many cells per action. Flag state doesn't cause incorrect scanning results if implemented properly, adjacent-mine counts are unrelated to this counter, and Board can be scanned any number of times.
